I’m 59, been farming these plots in Quzhou since I was a teenager. My father and grandfather did the same thing—wheat in the winter, corn in the summer. I went to primary school, enough to read labels and keep simple accounts, but I learned farming from watching and doing. The land here is flat, the soil is loam, and the water table is dropping, so I can’t waste water. I’m not one for fancy experiments; I stick to the rotation that pays the rent and feeds the family. Last year the wheat price was steady and the corn price didn’t collapse, so I’m not changing the main plan. I have about 4 mu of good land.

Here is what I will do:

1. **Winter wheat** on all 4 mu. I’ll plant the improved variety “Jimai 22” or whatever the seed shop recommends this year—it’s what my neighbors use and it resists lodging. I’ll plough once after the corn harvest, spread base fertilizer (compound fertilizer with N-P-K), then rotary till and sow in mid-October. I’ll irrigate four times: the overwintering water in late November, the green-up water in March, the jointing water in April, and one more at grain filling in May. I’ll top-dress urea twice. For pests and weeds, I’ll spray herbicide once in early spring and fungicide/insecticide once if I see aphids or rust.

2. **Summer corn** on the same 4 mu right after wheat harvest in early June. I’ll use a hybrid corn seed—probably “Zhengdan 958” or the local equivalent—because it gives the highest yield and the seed dealer gives credit. I won’t deep plough; I’ll do rotary tillage or no-till sowing if the stubble isn’t too thick. I’ll irrigate twice: once at the joint stage and once at filling, because water is expensive now. I’ll side-dress nitrogen at the big-flush stage. I’ll spray pesticides twice, once for weeds and once for corn borer if the county ag-station says the forecast is bad.

I won’t plant vegetables or cotton this year. Prices for cotton have been low for years, and vegetables need too much labor and market access. My back isn’t what it used to be, and my son works in the city, so I keep it simple.
